title: Throwing a Ball on the Moon
learningObjectives: Explain that a Moon throw has no drag and follows purely ballistic flight.
Describe how horizontal speed stays constant while vertical speed decreases under gravity.
Calculate maximum height from vertical speed and gravity using ymax = V0^2 / (2 * g).

sources.title: Throwing a ball on the Moon (project-authored test text)
sources.attribution: Written by the Make knowledge interactive project team for testing.

evidence.quote: On the Moon there is no air, so a thrown ball feels no drag at all.

explanations.text: A thrown ball on the Moon feels no drag because there is no air, so its flight is purely ballistic.

evidence.quote: Nothing pushes the ball sideways, so the horizontal speed stays U0 for the whole flight and the ball moves x = U0 * t across the ground.
Vertically, gravity slows the ball at a steady rate g.

explanations.text: Horizontal speed stays U0 with distance x = U0 * t, while gravity steadily slows the vertical motion.

evidence.quote: Putting that time into the height equation gives the highest point: ymax = V0^2 / (2 * g).
Because g on the Moon is about six times smaller, the same throw rises about six times higher than on Earth.

explanations.text: Peak height is ymax = V0^2 / (2 * g) at the moment vertical speed reaches zero, so smaller Moon gravity gives a higher rise.

predictions.prompt: Throw a ball on the Moon where g = 1.62 m/s^2 with horizontal speed 8 m/s and vertical speed 10 m/s. How high will it go?
Repeat the same 8 m/s horizontal and 10 m/s vertical throw with Earth gravity g = 9.8 m/s^2. How high will it go?
Toss a ball on the Moon with horizontal speed 12 m/s and lower vertical speed 6 m/s. How high will it go?
